    ABOUT THE ANALYSIS

    Forecasting models, exploration, preparation & statistical methodology

    Display, guided reading and printing

    Choose Light, Dark or Report in the header; this browser remembers the theme. Show settings opens the setup drawer. After a run, the summary ribbon offers Re-run and Export. Guided mode is off by default; enable it to walk through data, exploration, models, forecast tests and inventory using the existing header steps (or the mobile step menu). Disable it to restore the normal tabs. Each guide opens What we understood; use the section buttons or Show all four to read the rest. Print report opens an A4-friendly Part 1 report with white chart paper and complete guides. Clear data is available in both setup and Data, with an in-page confirmation.

    Every step in Demand Forecast Lab runs on a strict chronological split so zero future information leaks into data preparation, feature engineering, parameter tuning, interval calibration, cross-validation, or model selection.

    Strict Chronological Data Split (Zero Future Leakage)

    1. Training (First 40%)SMA window, SARIMA AIC search, Ridge/RF fit & MASE scaling
    2. Validation (Next 26.7%)Selects winning model, Top-3 Ensemble & 80%/95% interval quantiles
    3. Final Test (Last 33.3%)Untouched out-of-sample evaluation & Diebold–Mariano tests

    Data exploration & preparation

    STL Decomposition (Period = 5 or 7)

    Splits demand into long-run Trend, selected-calendar weekly Seasonal swing, and irregular Residual line (Graph 17_stl_decomposition).

    Stationarity Tests (ADF & KPSS)

    Runs Augmented Dickey–Fuller and KPSS on both level and first difference Δy across chronological lines (Graph 18_stationarity).

    Distribution & ACF/PACF

    Reports a frequency bar histogram with mean, median, IQR, and skewness (Graph 19_distribution), plus ACF/PACF stems to lag 20 (Graph 20_demand_acf_pacf).

    Causal Blank & Outlier Prep

    Fills blank cells causally via linear interpolation or weekday median, and flags one-step residual spikes after a 25-day warm-up without touching future rows.

    Descriptive supplementary charts

    CV-by-fold heatmap, demand by week and weekday, actual-versus-forecast scatter, and weekday error-direction counts add context without changing any forecast. The error-direction matrix requires at least 20 final-test rows. The finding section opens first; use the section buttons or Show all four for the complete guide.

    Forecasting models compared (up to 10 models)

    1. Moving average (SMA)
    Averages the most recent 3, 5, 7, or 10 observations (window selected on training data only).
    2. Exponential smoothing (SES)
    Estimates the level smoothing parameter α and initial level by minimizing one-step squared error on available history.
    3. Weekday regression (OLS)
    Fits an intercept, one indicator for each non-reference day in the selected five- or seven-day calendar, and lag-1 demand via ordinary least squares.
    4. Weekday naive
    Repeats the most recent observed value from the same weekday as a seasonal benchmark.
    5. Holt’s linear trend
    Double exponential smoothing that tracks both an evolving level and an additive linear trend slope.
    6. Ridge regression (richer features + single tuning pass)
    Uses lags 1 to 5, rolling means of the last 5 and 10 days, selected-calendar day indicators, and a trend index—plus week-of-month and month-end flag when real calendar dates are provided. Tuned once on the training/validation split over a 10-point log-spaced penalty grid (10^-3 to 10^3).
    7. Random Forest regression (richer features + single tuning pass)
    Uses the same richer feature set, tuned once on the training/validation split over 8 settings (n_estimators ∈ {50, 100}, max_depth ∈ {3, 6}, min_samples_leaf ∈ {1, 3}, random_state = 42). Reports both validation permutation importance and impurity importance (Graph 16_feature_importance).
    8. Holt–Winters seasonal (period = 5 or 7, via statsmodels)
    Triple exponential smoothing uses the selected operating calendar as its seasonal period, with additive or multiplicative seasonality and an optional damped trend.
    9. SARIMA (period = 5, via statsmodels)
    Seasonal ARIMA with period 5 selected once by AIC on the training split over 16 candidates, skipping non-convergent candidates and updating state with new observations without refitting inside a rolling block.
    10. Top-3 validation ensemble
    Equal-weight average (1/3 each) of the top 3 individual models selected strictly by validation MAE.

    Python runs in a browser worker via Pyodide (v314.0.7, including statsmodels 0.14.6 and scikit-learn). Original sample data: UCI Daily Demand Forecasting Orders (CC BY 4.0). Reference: Forecasting: Principles and Practice.

    USER GUIDE & TROUBLESHOOTING

    How to use Demand Forecast Lab

    Step 1: Load Your CSV/TSV

    Upload a comma, semicolon, or tab-separated file with 40–2,500 chronological daily rows, select Monday–Friday or all seven days, or click Load project dataset (sample.csv).

    Step 2: Pick Data Type & Unit

    Select your data type (e.g. Orders, Sales, Production) and unit so all charts and tables avoid duplicate labels.

    Step 3: Read the Charts

    Each chart uses an appropriate visual form and four reading-guide sections: What it is, How to see & read it, What we understood, and What to do next.

    Step 4: Optional EOQ & Schedule

    Open Part 2: EOQ & Purchase Plan to compute EOQ and order dates. Giving a service level (%) is optional—leave it blank for 0 safety stock.

    1. Opening the website

    Open the deployed website in a modern browser. The first analysis needs an internet connection while the browser loads Pyodide and the scientific Python packages.

    2. Accepted input data format & blank/outlier handling

    Upload a CSV or TSV file (up to 50 MB) containing 40 to 2,500 rows in chronological order. Choose Monday–Friday for operating-day series or All seven days for calendar-daily series.

    DemandWeekdayNotes (how the site reads it)
    285.0MondayRow 1 — oldest operating day (Mon–Fri name, code 2–6, or YYYY-MM-DD date)
    230.35TuesdayRow 2 — consecutive operating day
    WednesdayRow 3 — optional blank demand value (imputed via interpolation or weekday median, or rejected)
    222.44ThursdayRow 4 — continues in chronological order up to 2,500 rows
    211.92FridayRow 5 — Friday is followed by Monday on the next operating row
